headline: Lenin died in January, Congress shut the door on most immigrants in May, and Coolidge spoke on the radio
texture: Lenin died on January 21 and the fight to replace him started immediately. Petrograd was renamed Leningrad five days later. Hitler was sentenced on April 1 to five years at Landsberg for the previous November's attempt on the Bavarian government, and served rather less than that.

The Immigration Act of May 26 set quotas by national origin, cutting arrivals from southern and eastern Europe to a trickle and barring most Asian immigration outright. On June 2 Coolidge signed the Indian Citizenship Act, which granted citizenship to Native Americans born in the United States. He won the election in November against John Davis, and Nellie Tayloe Ross of Wyoming was elected the first woman governor in the country.

The Sea Hawk was the year's biggest at two million dollars in rentals, ahead of Harold Lloyd in Girl Shy and Douglas Fairbanks in The Thief of Bagdad. The first Winter Olympics opened at Chamonix on January 25 and the summer games opened in Paris on May 4. Coolidge became the first president heard on radio from the White House. Woodrow Wilson died on February 3, eighteen months out of office, and Puccini died in November leaving Turandot unfinished.
